svg.title: Tiemperos calling the rain at Popocatépetl and Iztaccíhuatl
svg.desc: Line drawing: villagers led by a tiempero pray at two flower-covered crosses at El Ombligo on Popocatépetl while storm clouds form over the volcanoes and rain falls on green maize fields; a strip below shows the ritual calendar from March to November.
svg.text: moist air forced up the slopes cools,
cave shrine with a large cross,
(I call out to them and they come)
villagers carry mole, tacos and fruit
to feed the volcano, then pray and sing
RAIN-FED MILPA · maize, beans and squash, ~2,200 m

g.text: FROM THE ETHNOGRAPHY
“Una nube, quieta o en movimiento,
es la expresión de una voluntad”
(a cloud, still or moving, is the expression of a will)
Julio Glockner, “La nube y el sueño”, Ciencias 90, 2008
CALLING THE RAIN
Popocatépetl and Iztaccíhuatl, Puebla–Morelos
WHO
Tiemperos, graniceros, aureros; in
Nahuatl quiapequi, “the one who makes rain”
HOW THEY ARE CHOSEN
Struck by lightning and survived (rayados),
or called by the volcanoes in dreams
WHAT THEY DO
Climb to caves and crosses, feed the
volcanoes, pray in Nahuatl, read the clouds
and steer hail away from the fields
THE OPPOSITE OF THE CANNON
The cannon tried to stop clouds; they invite them

svg.text: THE RITUAL YEAR FOLLOWS THE RAINY SEASON
in Puebla almost all rain falls from May to October
Don Goyo’s saint’s day, deep in the
dry season. Tiemperos climb with food
Crosses are placed on peaks and at
springs to ask for rain. The first
height of the rains and the hail
thanks for the harvest and close

g.text: HORTON STEPS
numbers from the hydrologic cycle plate
moist air rises up the volcano and builds cloud
claimed: the tiempero calls cloud and rain, turns hail
rain falls on the slopes and the milpa
milpa: soaks in, held in soil, breathed out
springs: crosses mark where ground water comes out
